title: Ban on using or distributing common pricing algorithms to restrain trade or coerce price adoption (AB 325)
requirement: Landlords, property managers and software vendors may not use or distribute shared rent-pricing software that draws on competitor data as part of an agreement to restrain trade. They also may not use or offer such software while pressuring others to adopt the rents or lease terms it recommends. Renters harmed by algorithmic rent-fixing can report it to the Attorney General or sue under the Cartwright Act.
key_value: Unlawful to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm (used by 2+ persons, uses competitor data) in restraint of trade, or to coerce adoption of its recommended prices or terms
coverage_conditions: Applies to any person or business, including landlords and apartment rental companies, that uses or distributes a common pricing algorithm in California. A common pricing algorithm is a method or software used by two or more persons that uses competitor data to recommend, align, stabilize, set or influence a price or commercial term. The law covers all products and services, including residential rents, and reaches every rental in California, with no limit by building type.
exemptions: End consumers are not 'persons' under the section. Single-firm algorithms that use only the business's own data are not covered (per secondary source).
citation: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729 (AB 325, Stats. 2025, ch. 338)
penalty: Cartwright Act remedies. Violations can be prosecuted as crimes (per Legislative Counsel's Digest). A secondary source says that under SB 763 (Bus. & Prof. Code §§ 16755, 16755.1) criminal fines reach the greater of $6 million or twice the gain or loss for corporations, and the greater of $1 million or twice the gain or loss for individuals. The same source cites civil penalties of up to $1 million in actions by the AG or a district attorney, and treble damages, injunctive relief and attorneys' fees in private suits.
quoted_span: (a) It shall be unlawful for a person to use or distribute a common pricing algorithm as part of a contract, combination in the form of a trust, or conspiracy to restrain trade or commerce in violation of this chapter.
merge_reason: Merged subsections (a) and (b) of § 16729 from the official statute text with a law-firm summary of the same AB 325 provision. The conduct-based condition (using a pricing algorithm) was removed from coverage, and the effective date comes only from the secondary source.

title: Application screening fee cap and refund rules (Civil Code § 1950.6)
requirement: A landlord can charge a screening fee only up to its actual costs. The fee can never be more than $30 per applicant, adjusted each year for inflation since 1998 (Berkeley lists $68.96 for 2026). The landlord can't charge a fee if it knows no unit is or soon will be available. It must give you an itemized receipt, refund any part it doesn't use, and give you a copy of your credit report within 7 days. It must also either consider applications in the order received and charge only the applicants it actually considers, or refund the whole fee to every applicant it doesn't pick, within 7 days of choosing a tenant or 30 days after you applied, whichever comes first.
key_value: $30 per applicant, CPI-adjusted annually from 1998 ($68.96 for 2026 per Berkeley)
coverage_conditions: Owners of residential rental property in California and their agents who charge applicants a fee to screen an application. Guarantors and cosigners count as applicants. No building limits.
exemptions: Does not override deposit and fee rules under federal or state housing assistance programs. Under the first-come process, no refund is owed to an applicant who was considered and denied for failing the landlord's written screening criteria.
quoted_span: In no case shall the amount of the application screening fee charged by the landlord or their agent be greater than thirty dollars ($30) per applicant.
merge_reason: All five candidates describe provisions of Civil Code § 1950.6 (the fee cap, receipt and credit-report rules, the ban when no unit is available, and the first-come-or-refund rule), so they were merged into one record. Effective date left null: the 2026-01-01 date in one candidate looks like an amendment or yearly adjustment date, not when the cap began.

title: Tenant Protection Act just cause for eviction and no-fault relocation assistance
requirement: Once you have lived in your unit lawfully for 12 months, your landlord can end your tenancy only for a just cause listed in the law, and the written notice must state that cause. For a no-fault cause, such as the owner moving in, taking the unit off the market, or demolition or a major remodel, the landlord must either pay you one month's rent as relocation assistance within 15 days or waive your last month's rent.
key_value: Just cause required after 12 months of tenancy; no-fault relocation = 1 month's rent
coverage_conditions: Residential real property in California, including mobilehome park units, once the tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied the unit for 12 months. If an adult tenant is added before 24 months, it applies only when all tenants have lived there 12+ months or at least one has lived there 24+ months. Housing must have a certificate of occupancy issued more than 15 years ago (mobilehomes excepted). It does not apply where a qualifying local just cause ordinance covers the unit; for example, the Los Angeles JCO/RSO governs instead where it applies. The 12-month tenancy requirement is about the tenant, not the building, so it is not used as a building coverage test.
exemptions: Transient or tourist hotels; nonprofit hospitals, religious facilities, extended care and residential care facilities; school dormitories; units where the tenant shares a bathroom or kitchen with an owner who lives there; owner-occupied single-family homes renting no more than two units or bedrooms (including ADUs/JADUs); owner-occupied duplexes where the owner lived in one unit at the start of the tenancy (neither unit an ADU/JADU); housing with a certificate of occupancy issued within the last 15 years (except mobilehomes); separately alienable units (such as single-family homes or condos) not owned by a REIT, a corporation, or an LLC with a corporate member, if the tenant got the required exemption notice under § 1946.2(e)(8)(B)(i); deed-restricted or subsidized affordable housing; mobilehome homeowners.
penalty: A termination notice that does not comply is void. An owner who tries to recover possession in material violation is liable for actual damages, plus attorney's fees and costs at the court's discretion. For willful conduct, oppression, fraud or malice, the owner can owe up to three times actual damages plus punitive damages. The Attorney General and the city attorney or county counsel may seek an injunction.

exemption_tests.description: Housing issued a certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years (except mobilehomes)
Two units in one structure where the owner lived in one unit as their principal residence at the start of the tenancy and still lives there; neither unit is an ADU or JADU
Separately alienable unit (single-family home or condo) whose owner is not a REIT, a corporation, or an LLC with a corporate member, where the tenant received the statutory exemption notice
Owner-occupied single-family residence where the owner rents no more than two units or bedrooms, including an ADU or JADU

conflict_note: Under subdivision (i), the section steps aside where a local just cause ordinance adopted on or before September 1, 2019 covers the unit, or where a local ordinance adopted or amended later is more protective and the city has made a binding finding saying so (for example, the Los Angeles JCO/RSO). A local ordinance adopted after September 1, 2019 that is less protective cannot be enforced. The current text was amended by AB 1529 (Stats. 2025, Ch. 203). One source gives a 2024-04-01 operative date for a later version of the section, but the just cause requirement itself dates from AB 1482 (2020-01-01). The section sunsets on January 1, 2030.
quoted_span: Notwithstanding any other law, after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause, which shall be stated in the written notice to terminate tenancy.
merge_reason: Merged the statute text and an LA agency page, which both describe the same Civil Code § 1946.2 just cause rule. I dropped the tenant-tenure condition from building coverage, added unit limits to the testable exemptions, and removed exemptions that cannot be tested.
interaction: Yields to BER-EVICT-01, LA-EVICT-01, LA-EVICT-02, SD-EVICT-01, SF-EVICT-01, SA-EVICT-01 where the local rule covers the unit.

title: State-set relocation payments for temporary displacement under 20 days
requirement: If you must move out temporarily for less than 20 days for capital improvement work, your relocation payment is set by Civil Code § 1947.9, not by a local ordinance. In San Francisco, the Rent Board lists $446.00 per day per household plus actual moving expenses for notices served from March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027.
key_value: $446.00/day per household plus actual moving expenses (SF figure, notices served 3/1/26–2/28/27)
coverage_conditions: Tenants temporarily displaced for less than 20 days. The sources describe this for San Francisco rent-controlled units.
conflict_note: For temporary capital improvement displacements under 20 days, the state statute governs the relocation amount instead of San Francisco Rent Ordinance (Admin. Code) § 37.9C.
quoted_span: The amount of relocation payments for temporary capital improvement evictions for less than 20 days is governed by California Civil Code Section 1947.9 and not by Rent Ordinance Section 37.9C.
merge_reason: Merged two San Francisco Rent Board pages that both describe the Civil Code § 1947.9 rule for displacements under 20 days. The 2026-03-01 date is an annual rate adjustment, so I did not use it as the effective date.

title: Housing Crisis Act relocation for lower-income households displaced by demolition

Code § 7260 et seq. In Los Angeles, the owner pays the state amount or the city amount, whichever is higher.
key_value: Relocation consistent with Gov. Code § 7260 et seq. for lower-income households
coverage_conditions: Protected units demolished for new housing development and occupied by lower-income households.

title: California statewide rent cap (Tenant Protection Act, AB 1482)
requirement: If your unit is covered, your landlord cannot raise your rent by more than 5% plus local inflation (CPI), or 10%, whichever is lower, over any 12-month period. The rent can go up no more than twice in 12 months. When a new tenancy starts, the landlord can set any starting rent; the cap applies to increases after that.
key_value: Lower of 5% + regional CPI or 10% per 12 months; at most 2 increases per 12 months
coverage_conditions: Residential real property in California, including units in mobilehome parks, whose certificate of occupancy was issued more than 15 years ago (rolling test; mobilehomes are excepted from the 15-year rule). The cap applies to rent increases on or after March 15, 2019 (February 18, 2021 for mobilehome tenancies). It does not apply where a local rent control law limits increases below this cap, such as the Los Angeles RSO.
exemptions: Housing whose certificate of occupancy was issued within the previous 15 years; affordable housing restricted by deed, regulatory agreement or other recorded document, or covered by a housing subsidy agreement; school or university dormitories; units under local rent control that limits increases below the state cap; owner-occupied duplexes where the owner lived in one unit at the start of the tenancy and still does, and neither unit is an ADU or JADU; separately alienable units (such as single-family homes and condos) not owned by a REIT, a corporation, or an LLC with a corporate member, if the tenant got the required written exemption notice; mobilehome homeowners.
penalty: The tenant can sue for an injunction and damages equal to the overcharge, plus attorney's fees and costs at the court's discretion. For willful, oppressive, fraudulent or malicious conduct, the court can award up to three times the overcharge. The Attorney General and the city attorney or county counsel can also enforce the law. The statute of limitations is three years, and any waiver of these rights is void.

exemption_tests.description: Housing that got its certificate of occupancy within the previous 15 years (rolling test)
Owner-occupied duplex: the owner lived in one unit as a principal residence at the start of the tenancy and still lives there, and neither unit is an ADU or JADU
Separately alienable single-family home or condo not owned by a REIT, a corporation, or an LLC with a corporate member, where the tenant received the required written exemption notice

quoted_span: an owner of residential real property shall not, over the course of any 12-month period, increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or a unit more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower,
merge_reason: I merged all four candidates into one record because they all describe Cal. Civ. Code § 1947.12: the statute text (D024), the LA housing page (D040), and two San Diego notices that only refer to the statute (D073, D077).
interaction: Yields to BER-RENT-01, LA-RENT-01, SF-RENT-01, SA-RENT-01 where the local rule covers the unit.

title: FEHA source-of-income protection, including Section 8/VASH vouchers, with income-test and credit-history rules for subsidy holders
requirement: A California landlord may not refuse to rent to you or treat you differently because of your lawful, verifiable source of income, including Section 8, HUD-VASH or other housing subsidies, and may not advertise "No Section 8." If you have a rent subsidy, any income test must use only your share of the rent, and a landlord who checks your credit must let you show other proof that you can pay, such as benefit payments, pay records or bank statements.
key_value: Source of income (including Section 8 and VASH vouchers) is protected; income test on tenant's share only; alternative evidence must be allowed in place of credit history
coverage_conditions: Owners of any housing accommodation in California, including apartments, single-family homes, condos and subsidized housing; also applies to property managers and tenant screening companies. 'Source of income' means lawful, verifiable income paid to the tenant, to the tenant's representative, or to the landlord for the tenant, including public assistance, housing subsidies, Section 8 and VASH vouchers. The credit-history and income-standard rules apply when the applicant has a government rent subsidy.
exemptions: An owner who lives in the home and rents to one additional person may exclude applicants based on protected characteristics, but may not publish discriminatory ads. Asking about the level or source of income is not discrimination. Landlords may still verify employment, ask for landlord references and verify identity.
citation: Cal. Gov. Code § 12955 (as amended by SB 329 (2019) and SB 267, Stats. 2023, Ch. 776)
penalty: CRD enforcement and lawsuits. Remedies include out-of-pocket losses, injunctions, access to the denied housing, emotional distress damages, civil penalties or punitive damages, and attorney's fees. File with CRD within 1 year or in court within 2 years.
quoted_span: (a) For the owner of any housing accommodation to discriminate against or harass any person because of the race, color, religion, sex, gender, gender identity, gender expression, sexual orientation, marital status, national origin, ancestry, familial status, source of income, disability, veteran or military status, or genetic information of that person.
merge_reason: Merged the statute text, CRD guidance and secondary descriptions of SB 329 (voucher protection, effective 2020-01-01 per secondary source) and SB 267 (credit-history alternative, effective 2024-01-01), because all are provisions of FEHA's Gov. Code § 12955.

title: Limits on use of criminal history in tenant screening (FEHA and Civil Rights Council regulations)
requirement: A California landlord may not reject everyone who has a criminal record, and may not consider arrests that did not lead to a conviction, sealed or expunged records, or juvenile records. If you are denied because of a conviction, the conviction must be directly related to your ability to be a good tenant.
key_value: No blanket criminal-record bans; arrests without conviction, sealed/expunged and juvenile records may not be considered
coverage_conditions: Most housing providers in California, including landlords and tenant screening companies, under FEHA and the housing regulations of the Civil Rights Council (formerly the Fair Employment and Housing Council).
exemptions: An owner who lives in the home and rents to one additional person is exempt from most FEHA rules.
citation: Cal. Gov. Code § 12955; Cal. Code Regs., tit. 2 (Civil Rights Council FEHA housing regulations on criminal history)
penalty: FEHA remedies: losses, injunction, emotional distress damages, civil penalties or punitive damages, attorney's fees.
quoted_span: Housing providers are also prohibited from having “blanket bans” of all people with a criminal history.
merge_reason: Merged the CRD official page and a secondary source on the same Civil Rights Council criminal-history regulations. The effective date comes only from the secondary source.

title: California security deposit law: one-month cap, 21-day return, deduction limits and photo documentation
requirement: A landlord may not take a security deposit (however labeled) of more than one month's rent on top of first month's rent, and may not call any deposit "nonrefundable." Within 21 days after you move out, the landlord must return what is left of the deposit with an itemized statement and receipts. The landlord may not deduct for ordinary wear and tear or damage that was there before you moved in, and must offer a walk-through inspection before move-out and photograph the unit to support any deductions.
key_value: 1 month's rent cap (2 months for qualifying small landlords); return within 21 days
coverage_conditions: Security deposits for residential rental property in California used as the tenant's home. The one-month cap applies to security demanded or collected on or after July 1, 2024. Since January 1, 2025, landlords must show proof that the repairs were done. Since April 1, 2025, landlords must take move-out photos before and after repairs or cleaning. Tenancies starting on or after July 1, 2025 also need move-in photos. Since January 1, 2026, a deposit must be returned electronically if the tenant paid electronically (AB 414). Since April 1, 2025, if a service member is charged a higher deposit, the landlord must explain why in writing and return the extra amount within 6 months if the tenant is current on rent.
exemptions: Small landlord exception to the cap: a natural person (including a family trust) or an LLC whose members are all natural persons, owning no more than two residential rental properties with no more than four units for rent in total, may charge up to two months' rent. This exception does not apply when the tenant is a service member. A landlord may also take an advance payment of at least six months' rent on a lease of six months or longer. Security collected before July 1, 2024 is not subject to the cap. Receipts are not required when repair and cleaning deductions total $125 or less, unless the tenant asks for them within 14 days. The move-out inspection notice does not apply when the tenancy ends under CCP § 1161(2)-(4). Electronic return is not required if the landlord and tenant agreed in writing to another method.
penalty: For bad-faith retention or demand, the tenant can get statutory damages of up to twice the deposit plus actual damages. For bad-faith noncompliance with the return and itemization rules, the landlord loses any claim to the deposit (§ 1950.5(m)).

exemption_tests.description: Small landlord (natural person, family trust, or LLC whose members are all natural persons) owning no more than two residential rental properties with no more than four units in total may charge up to two months' rent; does not apply to service-member tenants.

quoted_span: a landlord shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to one month’s rent, in addition to any rent for the first month paid on or before initial occupancy.
merge_reason: All 13 candidates describe provisions of Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5 (AB 12 cap, return deadline, deductions, inspection, photos, service-member and electronic-return amendments), so they merge into one record citing the statute text from D025.

title: Licensed broker fee disclosure to prospective tenants
requirement: Only a licensed broker may charge a prospective tenant a fee for finding an apartment. At the first personal meeting, the broker must tell you in writing the fee amount, when and how it is paid, and whether it depends on a lease being signed.
key_value: Written fee disclosure at first personal meeting; broker must be licensed
coverage_conditions: Real estate brokers and salespeople who deal with prospective tenants in Massachusetts. The only source is secondary and does not cover the 2025 change on who pays the broker fee (see M.G.L. c. 112, § 87DDD1/2).
quoted_span: In addition to holding a valid license, the broker has to tell the applicant in writing the amount of the broker’s fee, the time and manner of payment, and whether it is contingent on the owner and applicant actually entering into a lease or rental agreement.
merge_reason: This is a separate regulation of the broker licensing board, supported only by a law-firm source, so it is kept apart from the statutes.

title: Broker fee paid only by the party that hired the broker
requirement: A rental broker's fee may be charged only to the party (landlord or tenant) who first hired the broker under a contract. If the landlord or the landlord's agent hired the broker, you cannot be made to pay the broker fee.
key_value: Broker fee paid only by the party that engaged the broker
coverage_conditions: Residential rentals in Massachusetts where a licensed real estate broker or salesperson is used to find a tenant or a rental unit.
citation: M.G.L. c. 112, § 87DDD1/2 (as amended by St. 2025, c. 9, § 43)
quoted_span: Any fee shall only be paid by the party, lessor or tenant who originally engaged and entered into a contract with the licensed broker or salesperson.
merge_reason: This is a separate statute (the broker licensing law, as amended in 2025) on who pays broker fees, supported by official text.

title: Limit on up-front charges at start of tenancy (no application fees)
requirement: At or before move-in, a Massachusetts landlord or the landlord's agent can only require first month's rent, last month's rent, a security deposit of no more than one month's rent, and the cost of buying and installing a new lock and key. Application fees, screening fees, and other up-front charges are not allowed, and neither is a broker fee paid to the landlord's agent.
key_value: First month + last month + security deposit (≤1 month) + lock/key cost; nothing else
coverage_conditions: All residential leases and tenancies in Massachusetts. Since the amendment effective August 1, 2025, the rule also covers agents of the landlord.
exemptions: Leases or rentals of 100 days or less for vacation or recreational purposes. Licensed real estate brokers may charge fees under separate rules (254 CMR 7; M.G.L. c. 112, § 87DDD1/2).
penalty: Damages. A secondary source cites Perry v. Equity Residential (2014), where a federal court awarded triple damages and attorney's fees for unlawful application fees.

title: Ban on retaliatory termination, rent increase, or change in tenancy terms
requirement: A landlord may not threaten or retaliate against you, for example with a termination notice, rent increase or major change in lease terms, because you reported code violations, took legal action under housing laws, complained in writing, or organized or joined a tenants' union. A termination notice (other than for nonpayment), a rent increase, or a major change in terms within six months of that activity is presumed to be retaliation, and you can recover 1 to 3 months' rent or your actual damages, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees.
key_value: 6-month rebuttable presumption of reprisal; damages of 1–3 months' rent or actual damages, whichever is greater
coverage_conditions: Tenants of residential premises in Massachusetts. Applies to any person or agent who threatens or takes reprisals.
exemptions: Termination notices for nonpayment of rent do not trigger the presumption.
penalty: Damages of at least one month's rent and up to three months' rent, or actual damages, whichever is greater, plus costs and reasonable attorney's fees. Any lease waiver is void.
quoted_span: The receipt of any notice of termination of tenancy, except for nonpayment of rent, or, of increase in rent, or, of any substantial alteration in the terms of tenancy within six months after the tenant has commenced, proceeded with, or obtained relief in such action
merge_reason: Only one candidate, from official statute text. It is kept as a single record for the anti-retaliation statute; the record does not give an effective date.

title: Statewide prohibition on local rent control (M.G.L. c. 40P)
requirement: Massachusetts cities and towns may not pass, keep or enforce rent control, so there is no state or local legal cap on rent increases in Massachusetts. A city or town that accepts Chapter 40P may adopt only a narrow, voluntary program in which the city pays owners the gap between market rent and controlled rent.
key_value: Local rent control prohibited
coverage_conditions: Applies to every city and town in Massachusetts. The only local rent regulation allowed is the voluntary, city-compensated kind described in § 4(a) to (c).
exemptions: A city or town that accepts Chapter 40P may adopt rent control only if: (a) owners may opt out after six months; (b) it does not regulate occupancy, services, evictions, condo conversion or removal of units, and it does not apply to units of owners with fewer than ten rental units or units with a fair market rent over $400; and (c) the city pays owners the difference between market and controlled rent from its general funds.
quoted_span: Section 4. No city or town may enact, maintain or enforce rent control of any kind, except that any city or town that accepts this chapter may adopt rent control regulation that provides:

title: Massachusetts ban on source-of-income discrimination (public assistance and housing subsidies)
requirement: A Massachusetts landlord may not refuse to rent to you or treat you differently because you receive public assistance or a housing subsidy such as a rental voucher. They also cannot do it because of the subsidy program's requirements.
key_value: Source of income (public assistance, housing subsidies, rental assistance) is a protected class in rentals
coverage_conditions: Any person furnishing rental accommodations in Massachusetts. The statute does not limit this to certain buildings.
quoted_span: For any person furnishing credit, services or rental accommodations to discriminate against any individual who is a recipient of federal, state, or local public assistance, including medical assistance, or who is a tenant receiving federal, state, or local housing subsidies, including rental assistance or rental supplements

title: Massachusetts security deposit law: one-month cap, separate bank account, interest, and 30-day return
requirement: Your landlord cannot charge a security deposit of more than one month's rent, and must keep it in a separate interest-bearing account at a Massachusetts bank, giving you a receipt within 30 days and a written statement of the unit's condition within 10 days. The landlord must pay you 5% interest a year (or the lower rate the bank actually paid), and must return the deposit plus interest within 30 days after your tenancy ends, minus only allowed deductions backed by a sworn, itemized list.
key_value: Max 1 month's rent; separate MA bank account; 5% annual interest (or the lower actual bank rate); return within 30 days; treble damages
coverage_conditions: All residential tenancies in Massachusetts where the landlord collects a security deposit or last month's rent in advance. Interest on the security deposit is owed when the landlord holds it for one year or longer.
exemptions: Leases or rentals of 100 days or less for vacation or recreational purposes.
penalty: If the landlord fails to put the deposit in a proper account, fails to return it within 30 days, or tries to enforce lease terms that conflict with the law, the landlord loses the right to keep any of it. The tenant can recover three times the deposit or balance owed, plus 5% interest, court costs and reasonable attorney's fees (§ 15B(6), (7)). If interest on last month's rent is not paid, the tenant can recover three times that interest plus costs and fees. If the yearly interest is not paid, the tenant may deduct it from the next rent payment.

merge_reason: All four candidates describe different parts of the same statute, M.G.L. c. 186, § 15B (the cap, how the deposit must be held, interest, and return), so they were merged into one record.

title: FAIR Act: ban on algorithmic rent-setting software that uses competitors' nonpublic data
requirement: Starting July 1, 2027, New Jersey landlords may not pay for or use a 'coordinator': software or an algorithmic device that sets or recommends rents, lease terms or occupancy levels using competitors' nonpublic data. No one may perform a coordinating function or take part in parallel pricing coordination. Tenants can report violations through the Attorney General's complaint portal.
key_value: Use of algorithmic rent-setting coordinators that use competitors' nonpublic data is banned from 2027-07-01; violations count as violations of the NJ Antitrust Act
coverage_conditions: Applies to all owners of residential rental units in New Jersey and their agents, representatives and subcontractors, and also to software providers, coordinators and anyone else. title: Security Deposit Law: 1.5-month cap, interest-bearing account, 30-day return
requirement: A landlord may not collect a security deposit of more than 1.5 times one month's rent, and any yearly increase in the deposit may not exceed 10% of the current deposit. The landlord must keep the deposit in an insured, interest-bearing New Jersey account, pay the interest to you each year, and return the deposit plus interest, minus itemized deductions, within 30 days after the tenancy ends. If you are displaced by fire, flood, condemnation or evacuation, the deadline is 5 business days.

The 5-business-day return applies when an official posts a no-occupancy notice or certifies that the displacement will last more than 7 days.

If the landlord fails to give notice or pay interest, the tenant may give written notice and apply the deposit plus 7% annual interest to rent. Misusing deposit money is a disorderly persons offense (fine of at least $200 and/or up to 30 days in jail, N.J.S.A. 46:8-25).

title: Los Angeles Just Cause Ordinance (JCO)
requirement: If you rent a unit in Los Angeles that is not under the Rent Stabilization Ordinance, your landlord can evict you only for a reason listed in the ordinance once you have lived there six months or your first lease has ended, whichever comes first. You cannot be evicted for unpaid rent unless you owe more than one month's Fair Market Rent for your unit's bedroom size, and a no-fault eviction requires relocation assistance.
key_value: Just cause required after 6 months' tenancy or first lease expiry; non-payment eviction only if arrears exceed one month's FMR (since Mar 27, 2023); relocation assistance for no-fault evictions

Protection starts once the tenant has lived in the unit six months or the original lease has expired, whichever comes first. Every eviction notice must be filed with LAHD within 3 business days of service. The Fair Market Rent non-payment threshold took effect March 27, 2023 and applies to both RSO and JCO units.
exemptions: Transient hotels, licensed care facilities, fraternity/sorority houses, the owner's roommate, some cooperatives, some nonprofit homeless or short-term substance-abuse facilities, some HACLA or government-owned properties, and units already covered by the RSO, which has its own just-cause rules. For a JCO single-family home owned by a natural person who owns no more than four dwelling units and a single-family home in the City, relocation assistance is one month's rent (per LAHD relocation page).

title: RSO just-cause eviction, landlord declaration and relocation assistance
requirement: Your landlord can evict you from a rent-stabilized (RSO) unit only for a listed reason. At-fault reasons include nonpayment, a lease violation, nuisance, illegal use or refusing access. No-fault reasons include owner or family move-in, a required resident manager, demolition or Ellis withdrawal, a government order, HUD sale or conversion to affordable housing. For a no-fault eviction the landlord must first file a Declaration of Intent to Evict with LAHD and then file the notice with LAHD within 3 days of serving it. The landlord must also make relocation assistance available within 15 days of the notice: for July 1, 2026 to June 30, 2027 that is $11,000 or $14,400 for eligible tenants and $23,150 or $27,400 for qualified tenants.

Mom and Pop properties pay reduced relocation for owner or relative move-in evictions. No relocation is due when replacing a resident manager or for natural-disaster hazards the landlord did not cause. Accumulated unpaid rent may be offset against relocation, except for government orders to vacate.

requirement: If your unit is covered by the Los Angeles RSO, your landlord can raise the rent only once every 12 months, and only by the percentage LAHD publishes for that year (3% for July 1, 2025 – June 30, 2026). Since February 2, 2026, landlords cannot add an extra percentage for utilities or charge a 10% increase when a dependent joins the household. A 10% increase is still allowed for an added tenant who is not a dependent, but only within 60 days of the landlord learning about that tenant.

title: Ban on algorithmic rent-setting devices using nonpublic competitor data (Prohibition of Anti-Competitive Automated Rent Price-Fixing Ordinance)
requirement: San Diego landlords may not use software that analyzes nonpublic competitor data to set rents or occupancy levels, and no one may sell or license that software to landlords. If your landlord does, you can sue for an injunction, damages, or civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation, plus attorney's fees.

exemptions: Software that publishes reports from public information or from aggregated nonpublic competitor data more than 90 days old, as long as it does not recommend rents or occupancy levels for future leases or renewals. Software used to set rents or income limits under local, state or federal affordable housing program guidelines.
penalty: Tenants can bring a civil action for injunctive relief, damages, or civil penalties of up to $1,000 per violation, with each month and each property counted as a separate violation. A tenant who wins is awarded costs and reasonable attorney's fees. Remedies are cumulative, and SDMC Ch. 1, Art. 2 enforcement also applies.

(b) It is unlawful for a landlord to use an algorithmic device to set rental rates

title: San Diego Residential Tenant Protection Ordinance – just cause for eviction and no-fault relocation assistance
requirement: A San Diego landlord may end a tenancy only for a listed at-fault cause (such as nonpayment, a lease breach not fixed after written notice, nuisance or criminal activity) or a listed no-fault cause (owner or close-relative move-in, withdrawal from the rental market, a government order, demolition or substantial remodel). The termination notice must state the cause. For a no-fault termination, the landlord must pay relocation assistance of two months' actual rent (three months if the tenant is 62 or older or disabled), either paid directly within 15 days of the notice or by waiving that much rent.
key_value: Just cause required; no-fault relocation of 2 months' rent (3 months for seniors 62+ or disabled tenants); 5-year right of first refusal after a no-fault eviction
coverage_conditions: Residential rental property in the City of San Diego, including rented dwellings in mobilehome parks, where the tenant has lawfully lived for more than 30 days. Fixed-term leases of 3 months or less are not covered. Housing whose certificate of occupancy was issued within the previous 15 years is exempt (this does not apply to mobilehomes). Relocation assistance is owed regardless of the tenant's income or length of tenancy.
exemptions: Transient hotels and occupancies of 30 days or less; housing restricted as affordable by deed, regulatory agreement or subsidy agreement (Section 8 voucher tenants are still covered); mobilehomes subject to the Mobilehome Residency Law; nonprofit hospital, religious, care and transitional housing; school dormitories; tenants who share a bathroom or kitchen with an owner who lives there; owner-occupied single-family homes renting no more than 2 units or bedrooms; owner-occupied duplexes (neither unit an ADU or JADU); separately alienable units (such as condos or single-family homes) not owned by a REIT, a corporation or an LLC with a corporate member, if the tenant got written notice of the exemption; housing with a certificate of occupancy issued within the previous 15 years. No relocation assistance is owed if a government agency or court finds the tenant at fault for the condition behind a vacate order.
citation: San Diego Mun. Code ch. 9, art. 8, div. 7 (§ 98.0701 et seq.)
penalty: Wrongful eviction makes the landlord liable for at least 3 times actual economic damages, plus injunctive relief, punitive damages and discretionary attorney's fees. Failing to pay relocation makes the landlord liable for at least 3 times the required assistance plus actual damages (§ 98.0709(e)). Noncompliant termination notices are void, and a violation can be raised as an affirmative defense in an unlawful detainer case. The City may also bring civil and criminal enforcement.

requirement: In San Francisco, landlords may not use, and vendors may not sell, software that analyzes nonpublic competitor rental data to recommend rents or manage occupancy for residential units. Tenants or the City Attorney can sue violators for damages, an injunction and civil penalties.

title: San Francisco Rent Ordinance just cause eviction and relocation payment requirements
requirement: A landlord can evict you from a unit covered by the San Francisco Rent Ordinance only for one of the 17 just causes in Section 37.9(a), and that cause must be the main reason for the eviction. A lease ending or a change of owner is not just cause. For no-fault evictions (owner or relative move-in, demolition or permanent removal, temporary capital improvement work of 20 days or more, substantial rehabilitation, or an Ellis Act withdrawal), the landlord must also pay relocation money.
key_value: 17 enumerated just causes. Relocation for eviction notices served 3/1/26 to 2/28/27: (1) for owner move-in, demolition, capital improvement or rehabilitation evictions, $8,245 per tenant, up to $24,733 per unit, plus $5,497 for each tenant who is 60 or older or disabled, or for a household with minor children; (2) for Ellis Act evictions, $11,110.05 per tenant, up to $33,330.13 per unit, plus $7,443.90 for each tenant who is 62 or older or disabled.
coverage_conditions: Covers rental units under the San Francisco Rent Ordinance. The eviction rules also reach some tenancies that are exempt from the rent increase limits: units that first got a certificate of occupancy after June 13, 1979, tenancies where Costa-Hawkins allows rent increases, and some units whose rent another government agency regulates. A landlord also needs just cause to take away housing services such as parking, storage or laundry. Relocation amounts depend on the date the notice is served and are adjusted every March 1.
exemptions: The sources do not list the units that are fully exempt from the eviction rules. Relocation for temporary capital improvement evictions of less than 20 days is governed by Cal. Civ. Code § 1947.9, not § 37.9C. A landlord may temporarily remove some housing services for soft-story seismic retrofit work if the landlord follows Section 37.2(r).
penalty: An unlawful eviction or attempted eviction may expose the landlord to substantial civil and/or criminal liability.
quoted_span: In order to evict a tenant from a rental unit covered by the Rent Ordinance, a landlord must have a "just cause" reason that is the dominant motive for pursuing the eviction.

title: Santa Ana annual rent increase cap (Rent Stabilization and Just Cause Eviction Ordinance)
requirement: In covered Santa Ana rentals, your landlord can raise rent only once a year, by no more than the lower of 3% or 80% of the 12-month CPI change, and not at all if CPI is negative. The cap is 2.87% for September 1, 2026 through August 31, 2027; if your increase is higher, you can file a Tenant Petition with the Rent Stabilization Office.
key_value: Lower of 3% or 80% of CPI change (0% if CPI negative); 2.87% for 2026-09-01 to 2027-08-31
coverage_conditions: Residential rental units in Santa Ana in buildings built on or before February 1, 1995, and mobile home spaces first offered for rent on or before January 1, 1990. The City publishes the allowed increase by June 30 each year, and it takes effect September 1.
exemptions: Residential buildings built after February 1, 1995, and mobile home spaces first offered for rent after January 1, 1990. Owners may petition for a fair-return increase above the cap. State Costa-Hawkins limits on local rent control, such as exempting single-family homes and condos, also apply.
citation: Santa Ana Rent Stabilization and Just Cause Eviction Ordinance
penalty: Tenants may petition the Rent Stabilization Office to review increases above the maximum allowed increase.

exemption_tests.description: Residential buildings built after February 1, 1995 are exempt from the rent cap.

quoted_span: Increase in residential rents are limited to the lower of 3% per year, or 80% of the percent change in the Consumer Price Index over the most recent 12-month period. If the CPI is negative, no rent increase is permitted.
merge_reason: Both official city pages describe the same Santa Ana rent cap ordinance, so they are merged into one record. The coverage cutoff and effective date come from D085.
